title: How to Use This Directory
readingMarkdown:
# How to Use This Directory

One public directory of AI tools listed more than fifty thousand entries by late 2026. New ones appear every day, and old ones vanish. In 2026 alone, OpenAI closed its Sora video app, Google announced the end of its Firebase Studio development environment, and a well-funded maker of AI wearables was bought and stopped selling its device.

A list cannot keep up with that, and a list is not what you need. You need a method: a way to decide, for a job in front of you, whether any tool deserves a place in your work, and which one. This chapter is that method. The next chapter is the directory itself, and the one after helps you assemble a small set of tools of your own.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A hardware store

Nobody walks into a hardware store and asks for "the best tools". They arrive with a job: hang a shelf, fix a leak. The job decides the aisle, and the aisle offers a few options to compare.

A directory of AI tools is a hardware store. Browsing it without a job in mind produces the familiar result: a dozen sign-ups, three subscriptions, and no change in how you work.

So the first rule of this unit is simple. **Start with the job, not the tool.**

### A tool is a hire

Choosing a tool resembles hiring more than shopping. A sensible employer does four things, in order.

```text
   ALL THE TOOLS IN A CATEGORY
              |
   1. JOB FIT        Does it do the job I actually have?
              |
   2. RISK SCREEN    Is it safe to give it my data? Can I leave?         <-- can veto
              |
   3. COST           What will it really cost over a year?
              |
   4. TRIAL          Does it beat how I work now, on my own tasks?
              |
       ONE TOOL, or NONE
```

Each stage can reject a candidate, and the order matters. Checking privacy before the trial means you never upload a client's documents to a tool you were going to reject anyway. Checking cost before the trial means you do not fall for something you cannot justify keeping.

"None" is a legitimate outcome. Often the best tool for a job is the general assistant you already pay for.

### Many tools, few engines

One fact makes the directory much less intimidating. Most AI tools do not contain their own AI. They are built on a small number of underlying models from a handful of companies.

```text
   +------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  SPECIALISED APPS    a writing tool, a meeting notetaker,        |
   |                      a slide maker, a support agent ...          |   thousands
   +------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  ASSISTANTS          ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot ...        |   a dozen
   +------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  MODELS              from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta,       |
   |                      and a few others, plus open models          |   a handful
   +------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

A specialised app adds a workflow, an interface, integrations, and a prompt around a model it rents. Sometimes that is worth paying for: a meeting notetaker that joins your calls and files the notes is doing real work. Sometimes it is a thin wrapper around something your assistant already does. A question to ask of every tool in the top layer is: **what does this do that my general assistant cannot do with a good prompt?**

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### A taxonomy by job to be done

The idea of organising by job comes from a theory of innovation known as "jobs to be done", set out by Clayton Christensen and colleagues: people do not buy products, they hire them to make progress on something. A job is conveniently written in one sentence:

```text
When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].

When a client meeting ends, I want to have the decisions and actions written up,
so I can send them the same day without replaying the recording.
```

That sentence already tells you the category (meetings and notes), what good looks like (decisions and actions, same day), and what to test in a trial.

The directory in the next chapter is organised by job.

| Job | Category | Typical question |
|---|---|---|
| Think something through, draft, ask | General assistants | "Help me work this out" |
| Find and check information | Research and search | "What does the evidence say?" |
| Write and edit | Writing | "Make this clearer in my voice" |
| Capture meetings, manage notes and time | Productivity and meetings | "What did we decide?" |
| Make pictures and designs | Image and design | "I need a visual for this" |
| Make or edit video | Video | "Turn this into a clip" |
| Make or clean up speech and music | Audio | "Narrate this" |
| Make slides and documents | Presentations | "Turn this into a deck" |
| Write and change software | Coding and app builders | "Build this for me" |
| Connect apps and repeat tasks | Automation and agents | "Do this every time that happens" |
| Analyse numbers | Data | "What is in this spreadsheet?" |
| Keep everything on your own machine | Local models | "Do this without sending my data anywhere" |

Several tasks belong to more than one category, and one tool often covers several. The table is a set of aisles, and is not a classification of the tools.

### Five criteria

Once you have candidates for a job, compare them on five things.

| Criterion | The question | What to look at |
|---|---|---|
| **Capability** | Does it do the job well on my material? | Your own test tasks. Demos prove little |
| **Cost** | What will it cost in a year, in money and time? | Price, limits, setup, and the cost of leaving |
| **Privacy** | What happens to what I put in? | Training use, retention, who can see it, certifications |
| **Lock-in** | Can I get my work out? | Export formats, and whether an export is complete |
| **Integration** | Does it fit where I already work? | Connections to your files, calendar, and other tools |

These can be combined into one number. Score each tool from 1 to 5 on each criterion, give each criterion a weight $w_i$ reflecting how much it matters to you, with the weights adding to one, and compute

$$
S = \sum_{i} w_i \cdot s_i \qquad \text{with} \quad \sum_i w_i = 1
$$

With weights of 0.35 for capability, 0.20 for cost, 0.20 for privacy, 0.10 for lock-in, and 0.15 for integration, a tool scoring 4, 3, 5, 3, and 4 gets

$$
S = 0.35 \times 4 + 0.20 \times 3 + 0.20 \times 5 + 0.10 \times 3 + 0.15 \times 4 = 3.9
$$

Two cautions keep this honest.

**The weights are yours.** A solo illustrator and a law firm will weight privacy very differently. Write the weights down before you score anything, because choosing them afterwards lets you arrive at whatever answer you already wanted.

**A sum can hide a fatal flaw.** A tool with brilliant capability and unacceptable privacy can still total well. So add **hard gates**: minimum scores on particular criteria that no total can override.

$$
\text{reject if } s_i < m_i \text{ for any gated criterion } i
$$

A common gate is "privacy must be at least 3". A tool that fails a gate is out, whatever its score.

### What a tool really costs

The price on the website is the smallest part. Over twelve months the **total cost of ownership** is

$$
\text{TCO} = 12 \cdot f + (h_{\text{setup}} + h_{\text{training}}) \cdot r + c_{\text{exit}}
$$

where $f$ is the monthly fee, the hours are the time you spend getting it working and learning it, $r$ is what an hour of your time is worth, and $c_{\text{exit}}$ is the cost of moving your work out if you leave.

A USD 20 tool with four hours of setup, for someone who values their time at USD 40 an hour, costs $240 + 160 = 400$ dollars in its first year, not 240.

The tool pays for itself when the time it saves is worth more than that. The **break-even** is

$$
h_{\text{break-even}} = \frac{\text{TCO}}{r}
$$

Here, $400 / 40 = 10$ hours in the year, or about 50 minutes a month. That is the number to hold a tool to, and it must be measured against how you work now, not estimated from a demonstration.

Two patterns inflate costs across a whole set of tools.

**Overlap.** Three tools at USD 20 a month, each bought for a different reason and all able to draft text, cost USD 720 a year. A 2026 industry report on software spending found that about 36 percent of the licences organisations pay for go unused. Applied to those three subscriptions, roughly USD 260 a year buys nothing.

**Annual plans.** A discount of 15 to 20 percent for paying yearly is only a saving if you use the tool for the whole year. In a field where products are replaced every few months, a monthly plan is usually the better choice until a tool has proved itself.

### The risk screen

Before any tool sees real work, answer six questions. The answers are in the vendor's privacy policy, terms, and trust or security page.

| Question | Why it matters | What a good answer looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Are my inputs used to train models? | Your material may influence future outputs, and may be seen by reviewers | "No" by default on the plan you will use, or a setting to switch it off |
| How long is my data kept, and can I delete it? | Retention is exposure | A stated period, and real deletion |
| Who can see it? | Human review, sub-contractors, other users in a shared workspace | Named, limited, and controllable |
| Has security been independently audited? | A claim is not evidence | A recent audit report or certificate, such as SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 |
| Will they sign a data processing agreement? | Required when you handle other people's personal data | Available as standard |
| Can I export my work? | This is the lock-in test | A complete export in a common format, which you have actually tried |

Consumer and business tiers of the same product often give different answers to the first three. Modules 3.1 and 3.10 showed this for Claude and Gemini.

For browser extensions, add a seventh question: what permissions does it request? An extension allowed to "read and change all your data on all websites" can see everything you do in your browser.

Organisations have fuller frameworks for this. The best known is the AI Risk Management Framework from the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, which arranges the work under four functions, govern, map, measure, and manage, and has a companion profile for generative AI. An individual does not need the framework. The six questions are its spirit in miniature.

Surveys suggest that many people skip this step. Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, covering 31,000 workers, reported that 78 percent of those using AI at work were bringing their own tools. If your employer has an approved tool, start there. If it has a policy, read it first.

### The trial

A tool that has passed the first three stages has earned a trial. A good trial is short, fixed, and judged against criteria written down beforehand.

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Time box** | One week. Put the end date, and the date to cancel, in your calendar on the first day |
| **Tasks** | Three to five real tasks from your own work, the same for every tool compared |
| **Baseline** | Do each task your current way first. Record the minutes and rate the result from 1 to 5 |
| **Criteria** | Decide in advance what counts as success, for example "at least 20 percent faster with no loss of quality" |
| **Data** | Nothing confidential until the risk screen is passed |
| **Verdict** | Keep, reject, or defer. Written down, with the numbers |

Two measurements summarise it. Over the test tasks, the **time saved** is

$$
\text{saving} = 1 - \frac{\sum t_{\text{tool}}}{\sum t_{\text{baseline}}}
$$

and the **quality change** is the average difference in your ratings:

$$
\Delta q = \frac{1}{n} \sum \left( q_{\text{tool}} - q_{\text{baseline}} \right)
$$

Include the time spent correcting the tool's output in $t_{\text{tool}}$. A draft that arrives in ten seconds and takes twenty minutes to fix has taken twenty minutes.

Research on why people adopt technology, known as the Technology Acceptance Model, finds that two perceptions predict whether a tool is still in use months later: that it is useful, and that it is easy to use. A tool that scores well and is a nuisance to open will be abandoned. Note during the trial whether you reach for it without being reminded.

### Complexity

Every calculation in this chapter is a handful of additions and multiplications. The expensive part is the trial, which costs a week of attention. The purpose of the first three stages is to make sure that week is spent on very few tools.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

The method fits in five short functions. First, getting from a task to a category.

```python
TAXONOMY = {
    "meetings": ("meeting", "minutes", "transcribe", "notes", "call"),
    "writing": ("draft", "edit", "rewrite", "proofread", "email", "blog"),
    "research": ("research", "sources", "evidence", "papers", "cite"),
    "image": ("image", "logo", "illustration", "photo", "poster"),
    "data": ("spreadsheet", "chart", "analyse", "csv", "forecast"),
    "automation": ("automate", "whenever", "every time", "workflow", "sync"),
}

def classify_job(task, taxonomy=TAXONOMY):
    text = task.lower()
    best, best_hits = "uncategorised", 0
    for category, words in taxonomy.items():
        hits = sum(1 for word in words if word in text)
        if hits > best_hits:
            best, best_hits = category, hits
    return best

for task in ("Write up the minutes after each client meeting",
             "Edit and proofread the monthly blog draft",
             "Whenever a form is submitted, sync the row to the spreadsheet",
             "Repair the office printer"):
    print(f"{classify_job(task):<14} <- {task}")
```

- **The taxonomy is data.** Categories and their trigger words sit in one table. Adding an aisle to the store is one new line.
- **The best category is the one with the most matching words.** A task about meeting minutes matches "meeting" and "minutes". Ties go to the category listed first, because only a strictly higher count replaces the current best.
- **A task that matches nothing is "uncategorised".** The printer is not an AI job. Not every task has an aisle, and saying so is more useful than forcing a match.
- **The third task shows the limits.** It mentions a spreadsheet and also "whenever" and "sync". Automation wins with two matches against one. A person would agree, and a slightly different wording could have gone the other way. Classification by keywords is a first sort, to be looked at.

Next, scoring, with gates.

```python
WEIGHTS = {"capability": 0.35, "cost": 0.20, "privacy": 0.20, "lock_in": 0.10, "integration": 0.15}
GATES = {"privacy": 3}

def weighted_score(scores, weights=WEIGHTS):
    if abs(sum(weights.values()) - 1) > 1e-9:
        raise ValueError("weights must add up to 1")
    return round(sum(weights[criterion] * scores[criterion] for criterion in weights), 3)

def failed_gates(scores, gates=GATES):
    return sorted(criterion for criterion, minimum in gates.items() if scores[criterion] < minimum)

TOOLS = {
    "Tool A": {"capability": 4, "cost": 3, "privacy": 5, "lock_in": 3, "integration": 4},
    "Tool B": {"capability": 5, "cost": 4, "privacy": 2, "lock_in": 4, "integration": 5},
    "Tool C": {"capability": 3, "cost": 5, "privacy": 4, "lock_in": 5, "integration": 3},
}
for name, scores in TOOLS.items():
    print(f"{name}: score {weighted_score(scores)}   failed gates: {failed_gates(scores)}")
```

- **The weights are checked.** If they do not add to one, the function refuses to produce a number. A score from weights that sum to 1.2 looks like any other score and means nothing.
- **Rounding removes floating-point noise.** Sums of decimal fractions can come out as 3.9000000000000004. Three decimal places are more than a 1-to-5 scale can justify.
- **Tool B has the highest score and is rejected.** It totals 4.1 against Tool A's 3.9, and it fails the privacy gate. This is what gates are for. Without one, the best-looking tool would also be the one that should never see a client's file.
- **Gates are separate from the score.** The two functions answer different questions: how good overall, and whether anything disqualifies it. Keeping them apart stops a strong total from talking you out of a veto.

Then, the real cost and the verdict of a trial.

```python
def tco_12_months(monthly_fee, setup_hours, training_hours, hourly_rate, exit_cost=0, annual_discount=0):
    fees = 12 * monthly_fee * (1 - annual_discount)
    total = fees + (setup_hours + training_hours) * hourly_rate + exit_cost
    return round(total, 2), round(total / hourly_rate, 2)

def trial_verdict(tasks, min_saving=0.2, min_quality=0.0):
    baseline = sum(task["baseline_minutes"] for task in tasks)
    with_tool = sum(task["tool_minutes"] for task in tasks)
    saving = round(1 - with_tool / baseline, 3)
    quality = round(sum(task["tool_quality"] - task["baseline_quality"] for task in tasks) / len(tasks), 3)
    met = (saving >= min_saving) + (quality >= min_quality)
    return ("reject", "defer", "keep")[met], saving, quality

print(tco_12_months(20, 4, 0, 40), tco_12_months(20, 4, 0, 40, annual_discount=0.2))
print("three overlapping tools:", 3 * 20 * 12, "a year, of which unused:", round(3 * 20 * 12 * 0.36))

def trial(baseline, tool, quality_before, quality_after):
    return [{"baseline_minutes": b, "tool_minutes": t, "baseline_quality": qb, "tool_quality": qa}
            for b, t, qb, qa in zip(baseline, tool, quality_before, quality_after)]

BASE = [30, 45, 20, 60, 25]
print(trial_verdict(trial(BASE, [18, 30, 22, 35, 15], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [4, 3, 4, 4, 4])))
print(trial_verdict(trial(BASE, [28, 44, 21, 58, 26], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [4, 4, 4, 4, 4])))
print(trial_verdict(trial(BASE, [35, 50, 25, 66, 30], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [3, 4, 3, 3, 4])))
```

- **`tco_12_months` returns the cost and the break-even together.** The second number is the first divided by the value of an hour: the hours the tool must save in a year to pay for itself. A USD 20 tool with four hours of setup costs USD 400 and must save ten hours.
- **The annual discount applies only to the fees.** Setup time is the same however you pay. With 20 percent off, the year costs USD 352. The saving of USD 48 is real only if the tool is still in use in month twelve.
- **`trial_verdict` counts how many criteria were met.** Adding two true-or-false results gives 0, 1, or 2, which indexes directly into reject, defer, keep. Both met is a keep. Neither is a reject. One is a deferral, which means: not yet, and say what would change the answer.
- **The first tool is kept.** It cut 180 minutes to 120, a saving of one third, with quality unchanged on average: one task got worse and one got better.
- **The second is deferred.** Quality rose slightly and almost no time was saved. It might suit someone for whom quality is the constraint.
- **The third is rejected.** It was slower and worse. A week's trial, costing nothing, prevented a subscription.

**Complexity.** Each function is linear in the number of items it is given, which is a handful.

### A one-page decision record

Whatever you decide, write it down. Six lines are enough.

```text
JOB          When ___, I want to ___, so I can ___.
CANDIDATES   The two or three tools considered, and the "do nothing new" option.
SCREEN       Training use / retention / export tested: pass or fail for each.
COST         12-month total and break-even hours.
TRIAL        Tasks, baseline minutes, tool minutes, quality before and after.
DECISION     Keep, reject, or defer. Review date. Cancel date if rejected.
```

In six months, when a newer tool appears, this page is what lets you compare it with what you have in an hour.

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**Tool hopping.** Trying a new tool every week feels like progress and produces none, because skill with any tool takes time to build. Pick one per job, use it for a month, and only then ask whether something else would be better.

**The demo is not the job.** A launch video shows the task the tool does best, on material chosen for it. Your documents are messier. Nothing substitutes for your own test tasks.

**Paying for the same engine three times.** Many specialised apps are a prompt and an interface around a model you already subscribe to. Before paying, try the job in your general assistant with a careful prompt. If the result is close, the app is selling you convenience, which may or may not be worth its price.

**"Best AI tools" lists are mostly advertising.** Many are written to earn a commission when you click through. Rankings on such pages reflect payouts more often than quality. Independent comparisons that publish their method are worth more, and your own trial is worth most.

**Lifetime deals.** A one-off payment for "lifetime access" to a tool whose running costs are monthly is a bet that the company will survive and keep serving you. Buyers of such deals report capped usage, older models, and closures. Treat the price as what you are willing to lose.

**The annual plan bought in a moment of enthusiasm.** A twelve-month commitment made on day three of a free trial is the commonest way to pay for an unused tool.

**Skipping the privacy page.** People paste client data into a free tool they found an hour earlier. Free tiers are the ones most likely to use your inputs for training. Run the risk screen before real data, every time.

**Browser extensions with sweeping permissions.** An AI helper that sits in your browser may be able to read every page you open, including your bank and your mail. Check the permissions and the publisher, and remove extensions you have stopped using.

**Tools disappear.** Products are closed, bought, and repurposed constantly, including ones from the largest companies. Keep your own copies of anything you make, in ordinary file formats, outside the tool.

**Export that does not export.** "You can export your data" sometimes means a file that omits half of what you put in, or a format nothing else reads. Test an export during the trial, when leaving is still cheap.

**Bringing your own tool to work.** Using a personal subscription for the employer's data can breach policy, contracts, or law, however good the intention. Ask what is approved.

**Scoring after you have decided.** If you already love a tool, you will find weights that make it win. Set the weights and the gates first, and let someone else see them.

**Measuring the first draft and not the finished work.** A tool that produces a draft instantly looks like a huge saving. Time the task to the point where the result is good enough to use.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** The directory is a hardware store, and the way to use it is to arrive with a job, stated as a situation, a motivation, and an outcome. Most tools are specialised apps built on a few underlying models, so the first question of any of them is what it adds to the general assistant you already have. Candidates pass through four stages in order: job fit, a risk screen covering training use, retention, access, audit, agreements, and export, a twelve-month cost with a break-even in hours, and a one-week trial on your own tasks against a recorded baseline. Tools can be compared with a weighted score, $S = \sum w_i s_i$, with weights fixed in advance and hard gates that no total can override. The trial is judged on time saved and quality change against criteria written beforehand, and ends in a recorded decision to keep, reject, or defer. The result is usually very few tools, and sometimes none.

**Question 1.** A consultant weights capability 0.30, cost 0.15, privacy 0.30, lock-in 0.10, and integration 0.15, with a gate that privacy must be at least 4. Tool X scores 5, 4, 3, 4, 5 on those criteria in that order, and Tool Y scores 4, 3, 5, 3, 3. Compute both weighted scores, apply the gate, and say which tool goes forward and why the gate matters here.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

For Tool X: 0.30 times 5 is 1.50, 0.15 times 4 is 0.60, 0.30 times 3 is 0.90, 0.10 times 4 is 0.40, and 0.15 times 5 is 0.75, a total of 4.15. For Tool Y: 0.30 times 4 is 1.20, 0.15 times 3 is 0.45, 0.30 times 5 is 1.50, 0.10 times 3 is 0.30, and 0.15 times 3 is 0.45, a total of 3.90. Tool X has the higher score. It also has a privacy score of 3, below the gate of 4, so it is rejected, and Tool Y goes forward. The gate matters because a weighted sum lets strength in one place pay for weakness in another. Tool X's excellent capability and integration outweigh its privacy score even though privacy carries 30 percent of the weight. For a consultant handling clients' confidential material, a tool with inadequate privacy is unusable however capable it is, and no amount of capability changes that. A gate expresses exactly this kind of requirement: a floor, not a preference. The consultant should also note what would change the decision. If Tool X offers a business tier with different data terms, it could be scored again on that tier.

</details>

**Question 2.** A tool costs USD 30 a month, or 20 percent less on an annual plan. Setting it up will take 6 hours, your time is worth USD 50 an hour, and moving your work out later would cost about USD 100. Compute the twelve-month total cost and the break-even hours on the monthly plan and on the annual plan. A one-week trial suggests the tool saves about 1.5 hours a month. Should you take it, and on which plan?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

On the monthly plan the fees are 12 times 30, which is USD 360. Setup is 6 hours at USD 50, which is USD 300, and the exit cost is USD 100. The total is USD 760, and the break-even is 760 divided by 50, which is 15.2 hours in the year. On the annual plan the fees are 360 less 20 percent, which is USD 288, so the total is USD 688 and the break-even is 13.76 hours. A saving of 1.5 hours a month is 18 hours a year, worth USD 900. That exceeds the cost on either plan, by about USD 140 on the monthly plan and about USD 210 on the annual one, so the tool is worth taking. The margin is modest, though, and it rests on a single week's measurement. If the real saving turned out to be 1.2 hours a month, 14.4 hours a year, the monthly plan would no longer break even. The sensible choice is the monthly plan for the first two or three months while the saving is measured on more work. The annual plan saves USD 72, and commits you for a year to a tool whose benefit is not yet established, in a market where a better option may appear in that time. Switch to annual once the saving has held up.

</details>

**Question 3.** A small charity wants an AI tool to draft replies to donor emails. A volunteer proposes a free tool found on a "top ten" list and suggests testing it on last month's real donor messages. Describe what is wrong with this plan and lay out a better one, following the four stages of this chapter.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Three things are wrong. The tool was chosen from a list of the kind that is frequently paid promotion, not from a statement of the job. It is a free tier, the kind most likely to use what is entered to train models, and nobody has checked. And the proposed test would put donors' personal messages, which may include names, addresses, and details of giving, into a tool before any check on what happens to them, which could breach the charity's obligations to its donors. A better plan follows the stages in order. Job fit: write the job as a sentence, such as "when a donor writes with a question, we want a courteous, accurate draft reply in our voice within minutes, so that a volunteer can check and send it the same day", and note that the charity's existing general assistant may already do this. Risk screen: for each candidate, read the privacy terms for training use, retention, and who can see the data, check whether a data processing agreement is available since donors' personal data is involved, and test an export. Reject anything that fails. Cost: work out the twelve-month cost including volunteers' setup time, and the hours it must save. Trial: for one week, use five representative emails with all personal details removed or invented, record how long a reply takes now and how good it is, do the same with the tool, including the time to correct its drafts, and judge against a criterion fixed in advance. Record the decision and a review date.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: Classify the Job, Score the Tool, Cost It, Trial It
interactiveLab.context: A five-person studio is about to choose tools from a directory of more than a hundred and wants a decision method it can repeat. You will build that method: a classifier that maps a task to a category, a weighted scoring function, a set of hard gates that can veto a tool, a twelve-month cost and break-even calculator, and a verdict from a time-boxed trial.
interactiveLab.starterCode:
"""
Lab: Classify the Job, Score the Tool, Cost It, Trial It
Standard library only. Complete the TODO in each step, then press "Run & Verify Step".
"""

TAXONOMY = {

steps.title: From a task to a category
steps.instruction: Implement classify_job(task, taxonomy). taxonomy maps each category to a tuple of trigger words. Lowercase the task. For each category, count how many of its words appear anywhere in the task text. Return the category with the highest count. If two categories tie, keep the one that comes first in the taxonomy, which means replacing the current best only when a count is strictly higher. If no word from any category appears, return the string 'uncategorised'. This is the job-first step from Section 2: the job decides which aisle of the directory to look in. [MOD-4.1]
steps.hintConceptual: Read the task and see which aisle's vocabulary it uses most. If it uses none of them, the honest answer is that this is not a job for any aisle.
steps.hintSyntax:
text = task.lower()
best, best_hits = "uncategorised", 0
for category, words in taxonomy.items():
    hits = sum(1 for word in words if word in text)
    if hits > best_hits:
        best, best_hits = category, hits
return best
steps.testAssertion:
assert classify_job("Write up the minutes after each client meeting") == "meetings", f"Got {classify_job('Write up the minutes after each client meeting')}"
assert classify_job("Edit and proofread the monthly blog draft") == "writing", "Four writing words appear in this task"
assert classify_job("Whenever a form is submitted, sync the row to the spreadsheet") == "automation", "Two automation words beat one data word"
assert classify_job("Repair the office printer") == "uncategorised", "A task that matches nothing is uncategorised"
assert classify_job("DESIGN A LOGO AND A POSTER") == "image", "Matching ignores case"
assert classify_job("Make a chart") == "data", "One matching word is enough when nothing else matches"
assert classify_job("draft an email about the chart in the spreadsheet") == "writing", "Two writing words and two data words tie: the category listed first wins"
assert classify_job("anything", {}) == "uncategorised", "With an empty taxonomy every task is uncategorised"
assert classify_job("water the plants", {"garden": ("water", "plants"), "office": ("desk",)}) == "garden", "The taxonomy argument must be used"
print("Step 1 passed: tasks are sorted into categories, and a task with no match is left uncategorised.")

steps.title: A weighted score
steps.instruction: Implement weighted_score(scores, weights). First check that the weights add up to 1, allowing a tolerance of 1e-9, and raise ValueError if they do not. Then return the sum, over every criterion in weights, of the weight multiplied by the tool's score for that criterion, rounded to 3 decimal places. This is the formula S = sum of w times s from Section 2. Compute it for the three tools in TOOLS and notice which one comes out on top. [MOD-4.1]
steps.hintConceptual: Each criterion contributes its score scaled by how much you care about it. The shares of caring must add up to the whole, or the total cannot be compared with anything.
steps.testAssertion:
assert weighted_score(TOOLS["Tool A"]) == 3.9, f"Tool A scores 3.9, got {weighted_score(TOOLS['Tool A'])}"
assert weighted_score(TOOLS["Tool B"]) == 4.1, "Tool B scores 4.1"
assert weighted_score(TOOLS["Tool C"]) == 3.8, "Tool C scores 3.8"
_q1 = {"capability": 0.30, "cost": 0.15, "privacy": 0.30, "lock_in": 0.10, "integration": 0.15}
assert weighted_score({"capability": 5, "cost": 4, "privacy": 3, "lock_in": 4, "integration": 5}, _q1) == 4.15, "Recall question 1, Tool X: the weights argument must be used"
assert weighted_score({"capability": 4, "cost": 3, "privacy": 5, "lock_in": 3, "integration": 3}, _q1) == 3.9, "Recall question 1, Tool Y"
assert weighted_score({"a": 5, "b": 1}, {"a": 0.5, "b": 0.5}) == 3.0, "Two equal weights give the plain average"
assert weighted_score({"a": 2, "b": 4, "extra": 5}, {"a": 0.5, "b": 0.5}) == 3.0, "Only the criteria that have a weight are counted"
def _refuses(weights):
    try:
        weighted_score({"a": 3, "b": 3}, weights)
    except ValueError:
        return True
    return False
assert _refuses({"a": 0.5, "b": 0.6}), "Weights that add up to 1.1 raise ValueError"
assert _refuses({"a": 0.5, "b": 0.4}), "Weights that add up to 0.9 raise ValueError"
assert not _refuses({"a": 0.1, "b": 0.9}), "Weights that add up to 1 are accepted"

steps.title: Hard gates that can veto a tool
steps.instruction: Implement failed_gates(scores, gates). gates maps a criterion to the minimum score that is acceptable. steps.title: Twelve-month cost and break-even
steps.instruction: Implement tco_12_months(monthly_fee, setup_hours, training_hours, hourly_rate, exit_cost, annual_discount). The total cost is the fees, plus setup hours and training hours together multiplied by the hourly rate, plus the exit cost. The break-even is the total cost divided by the hourly rate: the hours the tool must save in a year to pay for itself. Return (total_cost, break_even_hours), each rounded to 2 decimal places. steps.title: The verdict of a trial
steps.instruction: Implement trial_verdict(tasks, min_saving, min_quality). Each task is a dict with baseline_minutes, tool_minutes, baseline_quality, and tool_quality. Compute the saving as 1 minus the total tool minutes divided by the total baseline minutes, rounded to 3 decimal places. Compute the quality change as the average of tool_quality minus baseline_quality over the tasks, rounded to 3 decimal places. Two criteria are then checked: the saving is at least min_saving, and the quality change is at least min_quality. Return a tuple (verdict, saving, quality), where the verdict is 'keep' if both criteria are met, 'defer' if exactly one is, and 'reject' if neither is. These are the trial measurements from Section 2. [MOD-4.1]
steps.hintConceptual: Was it faster by enough, and was the work at least as good? Yes to both is a keep, no to both is a reject, and one of each means you have not learned enough yet.
steps.hintSyntax:
baseline = sum(task["baseline_minutes"] for task in tasks)
with_tool = sum(task["tool_minutes"] for task in tasks)
saving = round(1 - with_tool / baseline, 3)
quality = round(sum(task["tool_quality"] - task["baseline_quality"] for task in tasks) / len(tasks), 3)
met = (saving >= min_saving) + (quality >= min_quality)
return ("reject", "defer", "keep")[met], saving, quality

"""
Lab solution: Classify the Job, Score the Tool, Cost It, Trial It
Standard library only.
"""

TAXONOMY = {
    "meetings": ("meeting", "minutes", "transcribe", "notes", "call"),
    "writing": ("draft", "edit", "rewrite", "proofread", "email", "blog"),
    "research": ("research", "sources", "evidence", "papers", "cite"),
    "image": ("image", "logo", "illustration", "photo", "poster"),
    "data": ("spreadsheet", "chart", "analyse", "csv", "forecast"),
    "automation": ("automate", "whenever", "every time", "workflow", "sync"),
}

WEIGHTS = {"capability": 0.35, "cost": 0.20, "privacy": 0.20, "lock_in": 0.10, "integration": 0.15}
GATES = {"privacy": 3}

TOOLS = {
    "Tool A": {"capability": 4, "cost": 3, "privacy": 5, "lock_in": 3, "integration": 4},
    "Tool B": {"capability": 5, "cost": 4, "privacy": 2, "lock_in": 4, "integration": 5},
    "Tool C": {"capability": 3, "cost": 5, "privacy": 4, "lock_in": 5, "integration": 3},
}


def trial(baseline, tool, quality_before, quality_after):
    """Provided helper: build the list of task records that trial_verdict expects."""
    return [{"baseline_minutes": b, "tool_minutes": t, "baseline_quality": qb, "tool_quality": qa}
            for b, t, qb, qa in zip(baseline, tool, quality_before, quality_after)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def classify_job(task, taxonomy=TAXONOMY):
    """A first sort by keywords. Not every task has an aisle, and saying so is more useful
    than forcing a match."""
    text = task.lower()
    best, best_hits = "uncategorised", 0
    for category, words in taxonomy.items():
        hits = sum(1 for word in words if word in text)
        if hits > best_hits:
            best, best_hits = category, hits
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def weighted_score(scores, weights=WEIGHTS):
    """Weights are fixed before scoring and must add up to 1, or the number means nothing."""
    if abs(sum(weights.values()) - 1) > 1e-9:
        raise ValueError("weights must add up to 1")
    return round(sum(weights[criterion] * scores[criterion] for criterion in weights), 3)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def failed_gates(scores, gates=GATES):
    """A gate is a floor that no total can override. Kept separate from the score so that
    a strong total cannot talk you out of a veto."""
    return sorted(criterion for criterion, minimum in gates.items() if scores[criterion] < minimum)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def tco_12_months(monthly_fee, setup_hours, training_hours, hourly_rate, exit_cost=0, annual_discount=0):
    """The price on the website is the smallest part. The break-even is the number of hours
    the tool must save in a year to pay for itself."""
    fees = 12 * monthly_fee * (1 - annual_discount)
    total = fees + (setup_hours + training_hours) * hourly_rate + exit_cost
    return round(total, 2), round(total / hourly_rate, 2)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def trial_verdict(tasks, min_saving=0.2, min_quality=0.0):
    """Criteria are fixed before the trial. Tool minutes must include the time spent
    correcting the tool's output."""
    baseline = sum(task["baseline_minutes"] for task in tasks)
    with_tool = sum(task["tool_minutes"] for task in tasks)
    saving = round(1 - with_tool / baseline, 3)
    quality = round(sum(task["tool_quality"] - task["baseline_quality"] for task in tasks) / len(tasks), 3)
    met = (saving >= min_saving) + (quality >= min_quality)
    return ("reject", "defer", "keep")[met], saving, quality


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for task in ("Write up the minutes after each client meeting",
                 "Edit and proofread the monthly blog draft",
                 "Whenever a form is submitted, sync the row to the spreadsheet",
                 "Repair the office printer"):
        print(f"{classify_job(task):<14} <- {task}")

    for name, scores in TOOLS.items():
        print(f"{name}: score {weighted_score(scores)}   failed gates: {failed_gates(scores)}")

    print(tco_12_months(20, 4, 0, 40), tco_12_months(20, 4, 0, 40, annual_discount=0.2))
    print("three overlapping tools:", 3 * 20 * 12, "a year, of which unused:", round(3 * 20 * 12 * 0.36))

    base = [30, 45, 20, 60, 25]
    print(trial_verdict(trial(base, [18, 30, 22, 35, 15], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [4, 3, 4, 4, 4])))
    print(trial_verdict(trial(base, [28, 44, 21, 58, 26], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [4, 4, 4, 4, 4])))
    print(trial_verdict(trial(base, [35, 50, 25, 66, 30], [4, 4, 3, 4, 4], [3, 4, 3, 3, 4])))

    q1 = {"capability": 0.30, "cost": 0.15, "privacy": 0.30, "lock_in": 0.10, "integration": 0.15}
    print("recall question 1:", weighted_score(dict(zip(q1, (5, 4, 3, 4, 5))), q1), weighted_score(dict(zip(q1, (4, 3, 5, 3, 3))), q1))
    print("recall question 2:", tco_12_months(30, 6, 0, 50, exit_cost=100), tco_12_months(30, 6, 0, 50, exit_cost=100, annual_discount=0.2))
